hints: Think about where Al and P sit in Period 3 and what type of oxide each forms, ionic lattice or discrete molecules.
Recall what must be broken to melt each type of structure, strong lattice bonds or weak forces between molecules.
Link the amount of thermal energy needed to break those different attractions to the very different melting points given.
walkthrough:
Picture the two different structures**
Imagine $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ as a huge 3D lattice of $\text{Al}^{3+}$ and $\text{O}^{2-}$ ions packed together and held by strong attraction in all directions. Now picture $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ very differently, as separate $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ molecules with strong covalent bonds inside each molecule but only weak attractions between neighbouring molecules.

Work out what melting actually breaks**
When $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ melts you have to break apart the ionic lattice itself, so strong ionic bonds between oppositely charged ions must be overcome. When $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ melts the covalent bonds inside the molecule stay intact, you only separate one molecule from the next, so only weak intermolecular forces are overcome.

Connect bond strength to melting point**
Ionic bonds are very much stronger than intermolecular forces. Far more thermal energy is needed to disrupt the $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ lattice than to separate $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ molecules, which is why $2072^{\circ}\text{C}$ is so much higher than $340^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Final answer: $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ has giant ionic lattice structure.
$\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ exists as simple discrete molecules.
Much more energy is needed to break strong ionic bonds than weak intermolecular forces, so $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ has much higher melting point.

hints: Substitute concentration units $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ for each term in the given $K_{\text{c}}$ expression and cancel top and bottom.
walkthrough:
Cancel the concentration units**
Put $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ into the expression: $$K_{\text{c}} = \frac{[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]}{[\text{CO}][\text{H}_2]^2}$$ $$\text{units} = \frac{\text{mol dm}^{-3}}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^2} = \frac{1}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^2} = \text{mol}^{-2} \text{dm}^{6}$$

hints: Use the 1:2:1 mole ratio in $\text{CO(g)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{(g)} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{OH(g)}$ to find moles of $\text{CO}$ and $\text{H}_2$ left when 0.280 mol of $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ has formed.
Divide each equilibrium mole value by the flask volume of $5.00 \text{dm}^3$ to get equilibrium concentrations in $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$.
Substitute the three concentrations into $K_{\text{c}} = \frac{[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]}{[\text{CO}][\text{H}_2]^2}$ and round to three significant figures with units from (b)(i).
walkthrough:
Find equilibrium moles using the mole ratio**
Start with 0.400 mol $\text{CO}$ and 0.800 mol $\text{H}_2$. Making 0.280 mol $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ must use up 0.280 mol $\text{CO}$ and $2 \times 0.280 = 0.560$ mol $\text{H}_2$ because of the 1:2:1 ratio. So left at equilibrium: $$n(\text{CO}) = 0.400 - 0.280 = 0.120 \text{ mol}$$ $$n(\text{H}_2) = 0.800 - 0.560 = 0.240 \text{ mol}$$

Convert to concentrations**
$K_{\text{c}}$ uses concentrations, so divide by $5.00 \text{ dm}^3$: $$[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}] = \frac{0.280}{5.00} = 0.0560 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$ $$[\text{CO}] = \frac{0.120}{5.00} = 0.0240 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$ $$[\text{H}_2] = \frac{0.240}{5.00} = 0.0480 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$ A common slip is to put moles straight into $K_{\text{c}}$, always convert first.

Substitute and calculate**
$$K_{\text{c}} = \frac{0.0560}{0.0240 \times (0.0480)^2}$$ $$(0.0480)^2 = 0.002304$$ $$K_{\text{c}} = \frac{0.0560}{0.000055296} = 1.01 \times 10^{3}$$ Give units from (b)(i), $\text{mol}^{-2} \text{dm}^{6}$, and three significant figures.

Final answer: At equilibrium: $n(\text{CO}) = 0.400 - 0.280 = 0.120$ mol, $n(\text{H}_2) = 0.800 - 2(0.280) = 0.240$ mol
$[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}] = 0.0560 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, $[\text{CO}] = 0.0240 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, $[\text{H}_2] = 0.0480 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$
$K_{\text{c}} = 1.01 \times 10^{3} \text{ mol}^{-2} \text{dm}^{6}$ to three significant figures.

hints: Remember what alone changes the value of $K_{\text{c}}$ and whether pressure or concentration is in that list.
walkthrough:
Separate position from value**
Increasing pressure will shift the equilibrium position to the right here because there are 3 moles of gas on the left and 1 mole on the right, so more $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ forms. But the value of $K_{\text{c}}$ stays exactly the same because $K_{\text{c}}$ only changes when temperature changes.
Final answer: No effect on $K_{\text{c}}$, as $K_{\text{c}}$ is unaffected by pressure and only changes with temperature.

hints: Focus on activation energy and think about a different pathway rather than the catalyst being used up.
walkthrough:
Picture the energy barrier**
A catalyst gives the reactants a different route to products that climbs over a lower activation energy hump. More molecules now have enough energy to react on collision, so rate increases while the catalyst itself is unchanged.
Final answer: Catalyst increases rate by providing an alternative mechanism with lower activation energy.

hints: Dehydration means removing water, so two $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ molecules must combine to give $\text{CH}_3\text{OCH}_3$ plus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, check atoms balance.
walkthrough:
Build the dehydration equation**
Removing water from two methanol molecules joins the two $\text{CH}_3$ groups through one O atom: $$2\text{CH}_3\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{OCH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Count to check: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$ on both sides, so it balances.

hints: Recall that $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ is an acidic oxide that reacts with excess water to give the phosphorus containing acid, balance P, H and O.
walkthrough:
Write the acidic oxide plus water equation**
$\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ reacts fully with excess water to form phosphoric acid: $$\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 4\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$$ Four P atoms need four $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ molecules, and six waters supply the $\text{H}_{12}$ and extra O to balance.
